# **2\. The Agentic SDLC** {#2.-the-agentic-sdlc}

The previous chapter established three things: AI has compressed the build step, the product surface hasn't changed, and the human role is shifting from producer to decision-maker. What's missing is a framework that operationalizes all of this — a concrete answer to the question: *if the old process no longer fits, what does the new one look like?*

The Agentic SDLC is that framework. It isn't a wholesale reinvention of software delivery. The stages will look familiar to anyone who has shipped software before. What changes is the division of labor within each stage — who owns what, where human judgment is irreplaceable, and where agents can carry the load.

The lifecycle has five stages: **Define**, **Shape**, **Build**, **Validate**, and **Run**. They are sequential in the main flow, but not rigidly linear — feedback loops between stages are a feature of the model, not a failure of it. Validation failures feed back to Shape. Production insights feed back to Define. The cycle is continuous.

[*(See A*![][image4]*ppendix)*](#appendix)

The gradient of ownership across these stages is worth noticing. Define is human-heavy: the business goal, the user problem, and the priority are fundamentally human decisions. As you move through Shape and Build, ownership shifts increasingly toward agents. By Run, agents handle the bulk of monitoring, triage, and alerting while humans hold operational accountability and make escalation decisions. This isn't a binary handoff — it's a sliding scale, and the most effective teams calibrate it deliberately for each stage. 

## **Defined** {#defined}

Define is where the work begins, and in an agentic shop, it's where the most consequential decisions get made. The purpose of this stage is deceptively simple: establish what you're building, for whom, and why it matters.

In a traditional process, the Define stage often got short shrift. Requirements were loose because the team knew they'd refine them during development. Specifications were thin because writing detailed specs felt like wasted effort when the code would evolve anyway. This worked — barely — when the build phase was slow enough to absorb ambiguity. Developers would encounter unclear requirements mid-implementation, walk over to a product manager's desk, hash it out, and adjust. The long build cycle provided a natural buffer for iterative clarification.

That buffer is gone. When an agent can generate a feature implementation in minutes, unclear requirements don't get caught during development — they get built. Confidently, completely, and wrong. The cost of ambiguity is no longer a slow conversation; it's a fast rework cycle.

This is why Define becomes the highest-leverage stage in the agentic SDLC. The human owns the business goal, the user problem, and the priority. These are judgment calls that require understanding of the market, the customer, and the strategic context — things that agents have no access to. But within this stage, agents can contribute substantial value: drafting requirements from a brief, expanding scenarios to cover edge cases the human didn't think of, generating acceptance criteria, and surfacing questions that a detailed spec needs to answer. The human sets the intent; the agent stress-tests it.

The practical output of Define is a specification detailed enough to drive agent-generated implementation without continuous human intervention. Not a waterfall-era requirements document — but not a two-line user story either. Think of it as the difference between giving directions to a local who knows the neighborhood ("head toward the park") versus giving directions to a capable stranger who will follow them precisely ("turn left on Elm, go 200 meters, the entrance is on the right past the red mailbox"). Agents are capable strangers. They'll follow your directions exactly — and that's both their strength and the risk.

The directions analogy covers structure: clear steps, explicit turns, precise distances. But real systems are full of knowledge that never makes it into directions because the people who work there carry it in their heads. The gate requires a keycode. The lobby floor is slippery when wet. The elevator skips the thirteenth floor. These aren't edge cases — they're the operational reality that experienced developers navigate instinctively and never think to document. Business rules that live in tribal knowledge, validation logic that "everyone knows," integrations that behave differently in production than in staging, regulatory constraints that only surface when a specific combination of conditions aligns — agents have no access to any of it unless you make it explicit.

This is the specification challenge that most teams underestimate. The obvious things — inputs, outputs, happy paths — are easy to specify. The hard part is surfacing the implicit knowledge: the business conditions that trigger different behavior, the constraints that aren't written down anywhere, the assumptions that are so deeply embedded in the team's understanding that nobody thinks to state them. A developer who's been on the team for two years absorbs this context through osmosis — code reviews, hallway conversations, production incidents. An agent starts every task from zero. What you don't specify, it doesn't know. And what it doesn't know, it will fill in with plausible defaults that are wrong in your specific context.

The quality of the specification determines the quality of everything that follows.

### Shape

Shape is where specification becomes architecture. The human takes the defined problem and decides *how* it should be solved at a structural level: which systems are involved, what the boundaries are, where the complexity lives, and what tradeoffs are acceptable.

This stage is where experienced engineers earn their keep in an agentic world. Architecture is judgment-dense work — it requires understanding not just the current problem but the codebase it lives in, the team that will maintain it, the scale it needs to handle, and the constraints that aren't written down anywhere. An agent can propose an architecture, but it can't know that the team tried a similar approach last quarter and it failed, or that the database can't handle the write pattern this design implies, or that the compliance team will reject anything that stores PII in that service.

The human owns the architecture, the constraints, and the decomposition of the problem into implementable pieces. This decomposition step is critical: the quality of agent-generated code correlates directly with the size and clarity of the task it's given. Research consistently shows that AI tools generate high-quality solutions for well-bounded, smaller tasks, but produce structurally shallow output when asked to solve large, complex problems in one shot. Shape is where the human makes problems agent-sized.

Agents contribute the implementation plan, edge case analysis, task breakdown, and dependency mapping. Given a clear architectural direction and a well-decomposed problem, an agent can produce a detailed implementation plan that accounts for interface contracts, data flows, error handling patterns, and sequencing. The human reviews this plan not for completeness (agents are thorough) but for *fitness* — does this plan fit our system, our team, our constraints? That's a judgment call that requires the contextual knowledge the agent lacks.

The output of Shape is a set of well-bounded, clearly specified tasks with defined interfaces, each ready for an agent to pick up and execute. Think of it as a construction blueprint: the architect decides the structure, and the builder executes within it. The blueprint constrains the builder's decisions in productive ways.

### Build

Build is the stage that AI has compressed most dramatically — and, counterintuitively, the one that requires the least fundamental rethinking. The mechanics of code generation are well-understood by now. Agents write code, refactor existing code, generate scaffolding, and produce documentation. They do this faster than humans, and for well-specified tasks, they do it well.

The human's role in Build shifts from producer to supervisor. The primary activities are review, steering, and exception handling. Review means reading and evaluating code you didn't write — a skill that, as discussed in Chapter 1, is now a core competency rather than an occasional task. Steering means intervening when the agent drifts from the architectural intent or makes choices that are technically valid but don't fit the system. Exception handling means catching the cases where the agent is out of its depth: novel integration patterns, security-sensitive operations, performance-critical paths where the "obvious" solution isn't good enough.

What makes Build work in the agentic SDLC isn't the code generation — that's table stakes. It's the quality of the stages that precede it. A well-defined problem (from Define) that has been decomposed into clear, bounded tasks with architectural guardrails (from Shape) produces dramatically better agent output than a vague ticket and a prayer. The teams that report the best results from AI-assisted development aren't the ones with the most sophisticated tooling — they're the ones with the most rigorous specification and decomposition practices.

This is the practical payoff of investing in Define and Shape: the Build stage becomes faster, more predictable, and produces fewer defects. It's not magic — it's the natural consequence of giving a capable but context-blind system the right instructions.

### Validate

Validate is where the agentic SDLC makes its strongest break from traditional practice. In most development teams, testing is the stage that gets squeezed — compressed by build overruns, under-resourced relative to development, and treated as a gate to get through rather than a quality function to invest in. The result is predictable: teams ship with incomplete test coverage, manual testing that can't keep pace with development velocity, and a validation process that catches bugs reactively rather than preventing them proactively.

In an agentic SDLC, this equation changes fundamentally. Agents can generate tests at the same speed they generate code — and they should. Test generation, test execution, regression checks, and coverage analysis are activities where agents excel. They don't get bored, they don't skip edge cases because they're running out of time, and they can generate test scenarios from specifications with a thoroughness that manual testing rarely achieves.

The human owns the quality bar, the risk judgment, and the release decision. These are irreducibly human responsibilities: deciding what "good enough" means, assessing whether the risk profile of a release is acceptable, and making the call to ship. But the *evidence* that informs those decisions — the test results, the coverage reports, the regression analysis — is agent-generated. The human is making a judgment call informed by comprehensive data, rather than making a gut call based on incomplete testing.

This is where the connection to Define becomes critical. If the Define stage produced detailed acceptance criteria and scenario coverage (which it should, with agent assistance), then the Validate stage can generate tests *directly from those specifications*. The spec becomes the test plan. Happy paths, sad paths, edge cases, boundary conditions — if they were captured in Define, they can be validated automatically in this stage. The loop from specification to validation becomes tight and traceable.

The aspiration is that 100% of tests flow from detailed specs to automated test generation without human intervention in the test-writing process. The human writes the spec. The agent writes the tests. The human decides whether the results are good enough to ship. That's a clean division of labor that plays to each party's strengths.

### Run

Run is where the software meets reality. Deployment, monitoring, support, and the continuous feedback loop that informs the next cycle of development. In traditional organizations, Run is often a separate world — handed off to an ops team, managed by different tools, governed by different processes. In an agentic SDLC, Run is integrated into the same framework.

Agents contribute monitoring, incident triage, alert summarization, and remediation drafts. The value here is in speed and coverage: an agent can monitor platform telemetry continuously, correlate signals across services, surface anomalies before they become incidents, and draft root-cause analyses that give the on-call engineer a head start. At higher levels of maturity, agents can propose and even execute remediation actions — rolling back a deployment, scaling a service, disabling a feature flag — subject to human approval.

The human owns operational accountability. When things go wrong in production, a human makes the decisions: what to prioritize, who to notify, whether to roll back or push forward, and how to communicate with customers. Agents can provide the data, draft the communications, and propose the actions — but the accountability sits with a person.

The Run stage also closes the loop. Production insights — what's actually happening in the real world — feed back into Define for the next iteration. Bugs become specifications. Performance bottlenecks become architectural constraints. Customer feedback becomes product requirements. The agents can facilitate this feedback loop by summarizing production data, categorizing incidents, and drafting specification updates — but the human decides what matters enough to act on.

## **Right Tool For Right Job** {#right-tool-for-right-job}

Across all five stages, a single principle holds: **humans own intent and judgment; agents own execution and coverage**. The human decides *what* to build, *how* to structure it, *whether* it's good enough, and *what to do* when it breaks. The agent drafts the requirements, plans the implementation, generates the code, writes the tests, and monitors the deployment.

This isn't a rigid rule — it's a gradient. Some tasks within each stage lean more human, others more agent. The balance shifts as teams mature, as agents improve, and as the organization builds trust through experience. But the principle provides a stable foundation for making those calibration decisions: when in doubt, ask whether the task requires judgment (human) or execution (agent).

The next chapter builds on this foundation. They address *how* to make each stage work in practice — specification-driven development, coaching your agents, human-in-the-loop quality gates.

# 

# **![][image5]**

# **3\. Best Practices** {#3.-best-practices}

The Agentic SDLC is a framework — clean, logical, and nicely diagrammed. Frameworks are useful. But they don't ship software. What follows are the practices that make the framework actually function in the real world — the things we've learned by running agentic development processes across real projects, with real teams, against real deadlines.

These aren't theoretical recommendations. They're the patterns that survived contact with production.

---

## **Specification-Driven Development** {#specification-driven-development}

The single highest-leverage change a team can make when adopting agentic development is investing in specifications. This sounds obvious. It is not. Most teams dramatically underestimate what "good enough" specification means when agents are doing the building.

### **Why Specs Matter More Now**

The concept of test-driven design is not new. Write the tests first, then write the code to make them pass. In practice, most teams never adopted it — not because the idea was bad, but because the economics didn't work. Writing detailed tests upfront felt like added overhead when the most resource-intensive, lengthiest step in the process was the coding itself. There was always pressure to just start building.

That economic argument has collapsed. With agentic development, the build step — historically the bottleneck — can compress from days to hours or even minutes. The constraint has moved upstream. The most expensive mistake is no longer slow code; it's building the wrong thing quickly. And the primary defense against building the wrong thing is a specification that leaves no room for misinterpretation.

[Thoughtworks identified spec-driven development](https://www.thoughtworks.com/radar/techniques/spec-driven-development) as one of the key new engineering practices of 2025, and for good reason. The dominant failure mode in agentic development isn't bad code — agents have gotten remarkably good at generating syntactically correct, stylistically consistent code. The dominant failure mode is correct code that implements an incorrect or underspecified requirement. The spec is now the source code, in a very real sense.

### The Spec Is Really a Pipeline

Treating “the spec” as a single document undersells what’s actually needed. In practice, the work of turning business intent into executable code passes through a chain of artifacts, each with its own job: **PRD → Specification → Architecture Plan → Epic → User Story → Tick**et. The PRD frames the problem and the outcome. The Specification translates that into precise expected behavior. The Architecture Plan defines how the system should change. Epics and Stories organize the work into meaningful increments. Tickets give humans and agents a bounded, executable task.

The order isn’t strictly linear — a Spec can expose a gap in the PRD, an Architecture Plan can reshape an Epic — but the principle underneath is progressive clarification. Each layer should narrow the range of reasonable interpretations, not just relabel the same ambiguity and pass it downstream. Most organizations don’t lack documents; they lack agreement on what each one is for, which is how a PRD ends up trying to specify behavior, or a ticket ends up re-litigating architecture:

| Document | Primary Job | Common Failure Mode |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| PRD | Define the problem, user need, outcome, and priority | Reads like a feature request; key decisions stay implied |
| Specification | Translate the PRD into precise expected behavior | Repeats the PRD without resolving ambiguity |
| Architecture Plan | Define how the system should change | Describes an implementation path without tradeoffs or constraints |
| Epic | Group work into a coherent product increment | Becomes a bucket of loosely related tickets |
| User Story | Describe a valuable slice of behavior | Generic “as a user…” statement with no real guidance |
| Ticket | Define an executable unit of work | Thin description that leans on tribal knowledge |

Of the six, the Specification carries the most weight. A PRD shouldn’t try to do its job — a good PRD explains what matters and why, not every edge case and data constraint. That translation used to happen informally, in a senior engineer’s head or a quick clarification meeting. With agents in the loop, there’s no one in the room to supply it on the fly, so it has to be written down: the happy paths, the sad paths, the edge cases, the business rules and data constraints, what’s explicitly out of scope, and how correctness will be verified. Get the Specification right and everything downstream gets easier — Architecture has something concrete to respond to, Stories sharpen, Tickets shrink, tests generate cleanly from acceptance criteria. Get it wrong and everything downstream becomes guesswork that turns into shipped code before anyone notices it was a guess.

This isn’t a return to waterfall. Waterfall tried to predict an entire system before anyone built it. This pipeline only has to make the next unit of work executable — a Specification doesn’t need to answer every question for the next six months, only the ones required to safely build the current slice.

### What Good Documentation Looks Like

Strong artifacts in this pipeline share five traits, regardless of length. 

* Accurate — the document reflects the current decision, not last week’s assumption; an Architecture Plan that still describes a sync API after the team agreed to go async is an active source of bad code, not a historical record.   
* Specific — “handle errors gracefully” is not specific; “return a 422 with a field-level error map, retry transient failures up to three times, surface permanent failures with the record ID” is.   
* Layered — each artifact has one job and stays in its lane, instead of cramming all the thinking into whichever document someone happened to be writing that day.   
* Traceable — a Ticket should connect back through Story, Spec, and PRD, so a reviewer can ask “does this match what we decided” instead of reopening a Slack thread.  
* Executable — a capable human or agent should be able to act on the document without oral tradition filling the gaps; if a Ticket only works when assigned to the engineer who sat in the planning meeting, it isn’t agent-ready.

### **The Practical Shift**

What this means in practice is that the team's creative energy moves earlier in the process. Product managers, architects, and senior engineers spend more time writing and refining specifications — collaborating with agents to expand scenarios, surface edge cases, and pressure-test assumptions — and less time writing and debugging code. The work is different, not less. And teams that treat specification as a first-class engineering discipline, rather than a box to check before "real work" begins, consistently produce better outcomes.

[Research presented at ICSE 2026](https://conf.researchr.org/home/icse-2026/ai-sqe-2026) demonstrated this measurably: incorporating architectural documentation and detailed specifications into agent workflows produced significant gains in functional correctness, architectural conformance, and code modularity. The spec quality and the code quality are directly correlated — there's no shortcut.

---

## **Coaching Your Agents** {#coaching-your-agents}

Agents are capable, fast, and tireless. They are not, however, clairvoyant. The gap between what an agent *can* do and what it *actually* does on your codebase, for your team, in your domain is entirely a function of the context you provide. [Andrej Karpathy popularized the term "context engineering"](https://x.com/karpathy/status/1937902205765607626) in mid-2025, describing it as "the delicate art and science of filling the context window with just the right information for the next step."  The label stuck because it captures something important: getting good output from agents is an engineering discipline, not a prompting trick.

### **What Agents Need to Succeed**

Through trial and error, we've arrived at a core set of context that agents should be provided to perform reliably in a development environment. This isn't optional enrichment — it's the minimum viable context for production-quality output:

**Coding standards.** Style guides, naming conventions, formatting rules, language idioms. Without these, agents generate code that works but doesn't match the team's voice. Every inconsistency creates review friction and accumulates style debt. The standards don't need to be exhaustive — a concise, opinionated document that covers the decisions your team has already made is far more useful than a comprehensive but generic guide.

**Semantic data model.** The domain model — entities, relationships, naming conventions, and the meaning behind them. Agents that understand your data model produce code that fits your system. Agents that don't will invent their own naming, create redundant structures, and subtly misrepresent domain relationships in ways that are hard to catch in review because the code "looks right."

**Business process definitions.** The workflows, rules, and logic that govern your application's behavior. This is where domain knowledge lives — the kind of context that experienced developers carry in their heads and new hires spend months absorbing. Agents need it made explicit. A payment flow has different rules than a signup flow. A healthcare application has different constraints than an e-commerce platform. If the agent doesn't know the business rules, it will generate plausible defaults that are wrong in your specific context.

**Model and prompt evaluation framework.** A structured approach to assessing whether agents are producing good output — not just once, but continuously. Models change. Prompts drift. What worked last month may not work next month. Teams need a way to measure agent output quality over time and catch regressions before they reach production.

**Skills and MCP integrations.** The tools, APIs, and integrations that agents need to interact with your development environment. File systems, databases, deployment pipelines, monitoring dashboards — agents are only as useful as the systems they can reach. Investing in clean tool interfaces pays dividends across every stage of the SDLC.

**Guardrails.** The boundaries that define what agents are *not* allowed to do. Don't modify production databases directly. Don't commit to main without review. Don't generate code that bypasses the authentication layer. Guardrails aren't a lack of trust — they're a recognition that capable systems operating at speed need explicit constraints, the same way a highway needs lane markers.

**RAG, Graph-RAG, and knowledge retrieval.** The mechanism for connecting agents to your team's accumulated knowledge — documentation, past decisions, architectural decision records, post-mortems. The pattern we see working best is starting narrow: one well-maintained, high-quality source (like primary API documentation or architectural decision records) rather than connecting every possible data source at once. Quality of retrieval matters more than breadth.

### **The Coaching Mindset**

The framing of "coaching" is deliberate. You don't configure an agent once and walk away — you iterate. You observe what it produces, identify where it falls short, and adjust the context. Maybe it's generating overly verbose error handling because the coding standards don't specify your team's preferred pattern. Maybe it's mismodeling a domain relationship because the semantic data model is incomplete. Maybe it's ignoring a constraint because the guardrails don't cover that case.

This is skilled, iterative work. The engineers who get the best results from agents treat context engineering the way a senior engineer treats mentoring a promising junior developer: invest upfront, give clear guidance, review the output, and adjust your coaching based on what you see. The difference is that agents learn from context within a session but don't carry that learning forward automatically — which is why the context artifacts (coding standards, data models, business rules) need to be maintained as living documents, not written once and forgotten.

---

## **Quality Gates** {#quality-gates}

This section focuses specifically on the structural checkpoints that ensure quality in an agentic workflow: the gates that code must pass through before it reaches production.

### **Why Gates, Not Just Reviews**

In a traditional development process, quality assurance is largely a continuous, informal practice. Developers test as they write. Code review catches issues through discussion. QA runs manual test passes. The process is human-paced and human-shaped, with quality emerging from the accumulated judgment of people who are close to the code.

In an agentic process, the speed and volume of code generation overwhelm informal quality practices. When an agent can produce a complete feature implementation in an hour, the old model of a developer spending a day reviewing it doesn't scale. Quality needs to be structural — built into the process as explicit gates that code must pass through, with clear criteria for what "pass" means at each gate.

### **The Gates**

The quality gates we've found most effective map to the transitions between SDLC stages. Each gate has a clear purpose, defined criteria, and a responsible party.

**Spec completeness gate** sits between Define and Shape. Before architecture work begins, the specification is evaluated for completeness: are outcomes defined, scope boundaries clear, constraints documented, and verification criteria specified? This gate can be partially automated — agents can evaluate specs against a completeness checklist and flag gaps — but the judgment call on whether a spec is "ready" belongs to the architect or senior engineer who will own the Shape stage.

**Architecture review gate** sits between Shape and Build. Before agents begin generating code, the architectural approach and task decomposition are reviewed. This is a human gate — it requires the contextual judgment that only someone who knows the system, the team, and the constraints can provide. The question isn't "is this plan complete?" (agents produce thorough plans) but "is this plan right for *our* system?"

**Automated test coverage gate** sits within Build, running continuously as agents generate code. Every pull request is evaluated against coverage thresholds, with code coverage used as a regression signal rather than a vanity metric. Teams using strict coverage gates on PRs make regressions visible immediately. This gate is fully automated — the agent generates code, the CI pipeline runs the tests, and the gate passes or fails without human intervention.

**Code review gate** sits between Build and Validate. Agent-generated code is reviewed by a human before it enters the validation phase. This is where the review skills described in Chapter 3 apply: reading code you didn't write, checking for architectural drift, evaluating security implications, and assessing whether the implementation fits the system. Teams using AI-assisted code review report reducing review time by 40-60% while improving defect detection rates — the agent flags potential issues, and the human makes the judgment call.

**Security and compliance gate** sits within Validate. Automated security scans, dependency review, license checks, and compliance validation run against the complete changeset. This gate is largely automated but with human oversight for flagged issues. In an agentic workflow, this gate matters more than ever: agents generate code from pattern-matching against training data, and those patterns may include known vulnerabilities or deprecated dependencies.

**Release readiness gate** sits between Validate and Run. This is the final human checkpoint: a deliberate decision to ship. All automated gates have passed, test coverage meets thresholds, security scans are clean, and the human with release authority makes the call. This gate is irreducibly human — it requires weighing risk, timing, business context, and confidence in a way that no automated check can replicate.

### **Gates as Trust Infrastructure**

The quality gates serve a second purpose beyond defect prevention: they build organizational trust in the agentic process. Teams that are skeptical of agent-generated code (and as we discussed in Chapter 1, skepticism is widespread) need evidence that the process catches problems. Well-defined gates with measurable pass/fail criteria provide that evidence. Over time, as teams see the gates catching real issues and letting clean code through, trust builds — not in the agent's infallibility, but in the system's ability to catch what the agent gets wrong.

This is the practical answer to the trust gap. You don't ask teams to trust agents. You ask them to trust the process — a process with enough checkpoints that nothing reaches production without being tested, reviewed, scanned, and approved. The gates are the mechanism that makes the agentic SDLC governable, auditable, and safe.

## Context Debt

Every engineering organization runs two decision systems in parallel. The official one is the artifact chain described earlier in this chapter: PRDs, specifications, architecture plans, tickets, ADRs, runbooks. The real one is Slack threads, meeting notes, hallway conversations, customer calls, and the senior engineer who “just knows how that service works.” Humans have always bridged the gap between the two — a developer reading a thin ticket knows there’s more context somewhere and goes and finds it. Agents don’t. They execute against whatever artifact they’re given. If the ticket is stale, they build the stale version. If a thread quietly overrode the spec, they never see it.  
That gap is context debt, and it deserves the same status technical debt already has: named, tracked, owned, and paid down deliberately — not discovered for the first time when an agent ships the wrong thing fast.

### Informal Decisions Are Still Decisions

The goal isn’t to eliminate informal decision-making. A customer escalation forcing a scope change, or a five-minute Slack thread resolving what a meeting would have taken an hour to settle, is normal and healthy. The problem is when the decision never makes it back into the artifact that governs execution. A PRD says one thing, a thread modifies it, the architecture plan never changes, and two weeks later an agent implements whichever document happened to be in context. The agent didn’t create that ambiguity. It executed against it.

### Ownership by Artifact

Context debt accumulates fastest when documentation quality is “everyone’s responsibility,” which in practice means no one’s. Each artifact in the pipeline needs a named owner accountable for its quality, not just its existence: Product owns the PRD — the problem, the rationale, the scope boundaries. Engineering owns the Specification and Architecture Plan — expected behavior, constraints, tradeoffs. Product and Engineering jointly own Epics and Stories. Tech leads and engineering managers own ticket readiness — whether work is bounded and executable without oral tradition. SRE, Support, and Engineering jointly own runbooks and operational notes.

The specific assignment can vary by org — the structures described later in this playbook should make this ownership explicit role by role — but every artifact needs an owner who knows what “good” means for it. If an agent ships bad output because a ticket was thin, the team should already know whose job ticket readiness was.

### Measuring It Through Rework

Context quality stays abstract until it’s tied to rework. When an agent’s output needs correction, classify why: a thin ticket, an incomplete spec, a missing architecture constraint, or a decision that was made informally and never wrote itself back into the artifact. The fix differs by cause — ticket standards, PRD-to-Spec translation discipline, decision-capture habits, architecture review rigor. This extends the measurement model described in the next chapter: alongside defect rate and rework volume, track rework cause, so every failure feeds back into improving the pipeline instead of just getting fixed and forgotten.

Most context debt isn’t created in the official documents — it’s created in the gap between when a decision is made informally and when, or whether, it gets written back. Distinguishing decision from discussion is the hardest part of this to operationalize: most of a Slack thread or meeting is discussion and can stay where it is, but the moment one changes expected behavior, scope, or a technical constraint, that decision needs to move into the durable artifact it affects.

---

These four practices — rigorous specification, deliberate agent coaching, structural quality gates, and disciplined context-debt management — are not independent ideas. They reinforce each other. Better specs produce better agent output, which requires less coaching correction, which passes through quality gates more cleanly, which leaves less context debt to manage. The investment compounds. Teams that adopt all four see dramatically different outcomes than teams that adopt one or two.

The next chapter shifts from *how to work* to *how to measure progress* — the maturity curve that helps teams understand where they are and what "better" looks like.

# 

![][image6]

# **4\. Adoption** {#4.-adoption}

## The Maturity Curve {#the-maturity-curve}

Agentic adoption is not a light switch. It's a gradient — a step-wise, piecemeal progression that looks different at every organization depending on their starting point, their codebase, their culture, and their appetite for change. There is no "go agentic" button. There is only the steady, sometimes uncomfortable work of moving your team from where they are today to somewhere meaningfully better.

What we've attempted to build with the maturity curve is a framework for honest self-assessment. Not a roadmap that prescribes a sequence of steps, but a mirror that helps a team see where they actually stand — across each stage of the SDLC — and recognize what the next level of capability looks like. The full matrix is available as a companion tool for detailed evaluation (see link at the end of this chapter). What follows are profiles of the five levels as we've observed them in practice.

| AI Maturity Curve | 1\. Non-Adopters / Skeptics | 2\. Individual Productivity Users | 3\. Standardized Tooling | 4\. AI-Augmented  | 5\. AI-Native  |
| ----- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- | :---- |
| **1\. Define** Define the problem, requirements, priority, and desired outcomes. | AI used to draft user stories and other design elements | AI generated PRD's | AI built functional, mini-app POC's | AI blows out comprehensive scenarios with acceptance criteria and sample data | AI used to estimate effort and help set priorities |
| **2\. Shape** Translate requirements into a clear implementation approach, including specifications, architecture, and task plan. | AI used for research | AI used as contextual sounding board | AI generates templated architecture plans | AI authors a proposed architecture | AI updates architecture based upon changes |
| **3\. Build** Go through the iterative process of writing, reviewing, and refining code. | AI writes code blocks. | AI changes code in place. | AI completes bounded repo tasks. | AI produces reviewable PRs/features. | AI runs a governed build workflow across agents, repos, tests, and review gates. |
| **4\. Validate** Ensure the solution works as expected through testing, performance checks, security gates, etc. | AI generated unit tests | AI generated functional tests | AI code reviews | AI integration and regression tests | AI fixes bugs |
| **5\. Run** Deploy, monitor, support, and surface issues for improvement. | Automated CI/CD with human triage | AI used to root cause issues | AI provides complete issue telemetry | AI monitors and reports on platform stability | AI proactively remedies potential issues |

### Level 1: Non-Adopters and Skeptics

This is the starting line, and it's where more teams sit than anyone in the industry likes to admit. AI tools may be technically available, but they aren't meaningfully integrated into how the team works. Individual developers might use ChatGPT to draft a user story or generate a code snippet, but it's ad hoc — there's no process around it, no standards for when or how to use AI, and no organizational expectation that anyone should.

The defining characteristic of Level 1 isn't resistance to AI — it's indifference to it as a *process* concern. AI might show up in the Build stage (an engineer pastes code into a chat window to get a refactoring suggestion), and it might show up in Run (someone asks an AI to help interpret a stack trace). But it's not woven into the workflow. There are no shared tools, no team-level practices, and no measurement of whether AI is helping or hurting.

Teams at Level 1 often have strong engineering cultures. They're not behind because they're bad at software — they're behind because the existing process works well enough that the disruption cost of changing feels higher than the marginal improvement. The risk is that "well enough" erodes as competitors at higher maturity levels begin shipping faster with comparable or better quality.

### Level 2: Individual Productivity Users — "Shadow AI"

Level 2 is where most of the industry landed in 2024-2025. Individual developers are using AI tools regularly — GitHub Copilot, Cursor, Claude, ChatGPT — and seeing real personal productivity gains. They're generating code faster, writing tests they wouldn't have written manually, and using AI as a sounding board for architectural questions. But the adoption is individual, not organizational.

The "Shadow AI" label is deliberate. Much of the AI usage at Level 2 is invisible to the team and the organization. Developers are using their own tools, with their own workflows, and making their own judgments about when AI output is good enough. There's no shared coding standards document that agents reference. There's no team-wide specification practice tuned for agent consumption. There's no quality gate that explicitly evaluates AI-generated code. The gains are real but fragmented, and the risks — inconsistent code quality, undisclosed AI-generated code in critical paths, no organizational learning about what works — are accumulating silently.

The transition from Level 2 to Level 3 is less about technology and more about organizational intention. It requires someone — a tech lead, an engineering manager, a CTO — to say: "We are doing this as a team, not as individuals. Let's standardize."

### Level 3: Standardized Tooling and Assisted Engineering

Level 3 is where agentic development begins to feel like a *process* rather than a collection of personal productivity hacks. The organization has made deliberate choices: standardized tools, shared configurations, team-level practices, and explicit expectations about how AI fits into the workflow.

At this level, Define starts to look different — AI is used to generate templated architecture plans and build functional mini-app POCs to test assumptions before committing to full development. Shape becomes more rigorous as AI generates architecture plans from constraints and the team reviews them as a starting point rather than starting from a blank page. Build is where the most visible change occurs: agents complete bounded tasks within repos, working from specifications and producing reviewable output. Validate gets its own upgrade — AI-generated code reviews supplement human review, and automated test generation begins to close coverage gaps. Run gains AI-powered telemetry that provides richer context for incident response.

The key characteristic of Level 3 is that the team has *standards*. There's a shared understanding of which tools to use, how to use them, and what quality looks like for agent output. Coding standards are documented. Agent context is managed at the team level, not left to individual preference. Quality gates include explicit checkpoints for AI-generated code.

What Level 3 doesn't have yet is true agent *autonomy*. Agents are still assistants — they help, they accelerate, but they don't own entire workflows end to end. The human is still in the driver's seat at every stage, which is appropriate for teams building confidence and trust in the process.

### Level 4: AI-Augmented Systems — Agent-Assisted Workflows

Level 4 is the transition point where agents move from assistants to participants. The distinction is meaningful: at Level 3, a human asks an agent to do something and reviews the result. At Level 4, agents are integrated into workflows that execute semi-autonomously — producing reviewable PRs and features, running comprehensive test suites, monitoring production stability, and surfacing issues with proposed remediations.

At this level, the practices described in Chapter 3 — specification-driven development, agent coaching, quality gates — aren't aspirational; they're operational. Specifications are detailed enough to drive agent-generated implementations without continuous hand-holding. Agent context is curated and maintained as a team discipline. Quality gates are automated where possible and structurally enforced where human judgment is needed.

The organizational shift at Level 4 is significant. The team isn't just using AI tools — they've reorganized their workflow around the human-agent division of labor. Define is a first-class engineering discipline. Shape produces agent-ready task decompositions. Build is primarily agent-executed with human oversight. Validate is driven by automated test generation from specifications. Run includes proactive monitoring with agent-proposed remediation.

Level 4 is where many strong engineering organizations are heading in 2026\. It requires real investment — in specification practices, in agent context, in quality infrastructure — but the returns are substantial: faster delivery, more consistent quality, and a team that spends its energy on judgment and decision-making rather than production.

### Level 5: Agent-Native Engineering Organizations

Level 5 is the horizon — the model that a small number of teams are beginning to demonstrate, and that represents the logical endpoint of the maturity curve. At this level, agents don't just participate in the workflow; they *run* it, with humans providing strategic direction, architectural governance, and judgment at critical decision points.

In a Level 5 organization, agents estimate effort and help set priorities in Define. They curate and evolve architecture based on changing requirements in Shape. They run governed build workflows across multiple agents, repos, tests, and review gates in Build. They autonomously fix bugs and close regression gaps in Validate. They proactively identify and remediate potential issues before they impact users in Run.

The human role at Level 5 is genuinely supervisory — not in the diminished sense, but in the high-leverage sense. Humans set the vision, define the boundaries, make the hard tradeoff decisions, and hold the organization accountable for outcomes. Everything else is agent-executed within human-defined guardrails.

It's worth noting that Level 5 is not a destination every organization needs to reach, or should rush toward. The jump from Level 4 to Level 5 requires deep trust in the agentic process, robust quality infrastructure, and a team culture that is comfortable with a fundamentally different relationship to code. For most organizations in 2026, the practical goal is to move from wherever they are today toward Level 3 or 4 — and to do so deliberately, with the practices and frameworks described in this playbook.

## Measuring Agentic Maturity {#measuring-agentic-maturity}

If you can't measure it, you can't improve it. But in an agentic SDLC, the harder problem is measuring the *right things*. The instinct — for teams and for the executives funding the tooling — is to ask: "Are we writing more code?" That question is worse than useless. It actively misleads.

More tokens consumed, more commits pushed, more story points closed — none of these tell you whether you're delivering more value, at better quality, with lower coordination cost. They measure *activity*, not *leverage*. And the difference between the two is the difference between a team that's getting better and a team that's just getting busier.

The [DORA 2025 State of AI-Assisted Software Development report](https://dora.dev/dora-report-2025/) documented this dynamic precisely. While AI adoption now positively correlates with delivery throughput — reversing their 2024 finding — it continues to negatively correlate with delivery stability. The report's core insight: AI doesn't fix a team; it amplifies what's already there. Organizations that measure activity optimize for the wrong things. They generate more code without improving the specifications, architecture, validation, and oversight that determine whether that code is any good.

This chapter provides a measurement framework designed for three audiences: the team that needs to know if their practices are improving week over week, the engineering leader who needs to know where to invest next, and the executive who needs to know if the investment in agentic tooling is paying off.

### The Activity Trap

Before describing what to measure, it's worth dwelling on what not to measure — because the vanity metrics are seductive, and nearly every organization falls for at least one of them.

**Lines of code generated** is the most obvious trap. An agent can produce thousands of lines of code in an afternoon. That tells you nothing about whether any of it should exist. Lines of code is a measure of output volume, not output value. In an agentic workflow, it often correlates *negatively* with quality — the teams generating the most code are frequently the ones with the weakest specifications, producing confident implementations of poorly defined requirements.

**Token consumption** feels like it should correlate with productivity. It doesn't. High token usage can mean a team is using agents extensively and effectively. It can also mean agents are spinning on poorly scoped tasks, regenerating output that keeps getting rejected, or being fed inadequate context that forces repeated correction loops. Without knowing what the tokens produced, the number is meaningless.

**Number of AI-assisted commits or PRs** has the same problem. More PRs merged tells you the team is shipping more units of change. It tells you nothing about whether those changes are valuable, well-tested, or architecturally sound. The DORA research found that organizations maintaining small-batch discipline — staging code across multiple reviewable PRs rather than shipping large AI-generated changesets — see better outcomes, even though their raw PR counts are lower.

**Story points completed** is a pre-existing problem that agentic development makes worse. If a team inflates story point estimates (consciously or not) to account for AI-assisted velocity, the metrics look great while actual delivery quality degrades. Story points measure estimated effort, not delivered value.

The common thread: all of these metrics measure *how much* without measuring *how well* or *to what end*. In an agentic world, the capacity to produce is essentially unlimited. The constraint has shifted to judgment, quality, and specification — and the measurement framework needs to shift with it.

### Four Dimensions of Agentic Measurement

A useful measurement model covers four dimensions. No single metric tells the whole story; the insight comes from reading them together, watching the trends, and noticing when one dimension improves at the expense of another.

#### Speed

Speed is the dimension executives care about most, and it's the one most likely to mislead if measured in isolation. The relevant metrics are not "how fast did we write code" but "how fast did we deliver a working capability."

1. **Cycle time** — the elapsed time from work starting to work shipping — is the primary speed metric. In an agentic SDLC, cycle time should compress as Build accelerates, but it won't compress as much as people expect if Define and Shape are underinvested. A team that generates code in an hour but spends three days clarifying requirements and reworking implementations hasn't actually gotten faster in any way that matters.  
2. **Lead time** — the elapsed time from a request entering the backlog to a working feature in production — captures the full pipeline, including the wait time before work starts. This is often the metric that reveals organizational bottlenecks: a team might have fast cycle times but long lead times because work sits in a prioritization queue for weeks before anyone touches it.  
3. **Time from spec to working feature** is the metric most specific to agentic development. It measures the end-to-end efficiency of the agentic SDLC pipeline: how long does it take to go from a completed specification to a validated, deployable feature? This metric rewards investment in specification quality (better specs → fewer correction loops → faster delivery) and penalizes teams that skip Define and Shape.

#### Quality

Quality metrics answer the question: "Is the software we're shipping actually good?" In an agentic workflow, this question has a sharper edge — because the speed of production can mask quality problems that only surface later.

1. **Defect rate** — defects per unit of delivered work — is the foundational quality metric. Track it over time, and track it by source: are defects coming from agent-generated code, from specification gaps, from integration issues, or from areas where human review missed something? The source distribution tells you where to invest.  
2. **Escaped bug rate** — defects that reach production — is the quality metric that matters most to executives and customers. A team can have a high defect rate in development (caught by quality gates) and a low escaped bug rate (nothing reaches users). That's a healthy system. The reverse — low defect rate in development, high escaped bug rate — means the quality gates aren't working.  
3. **Rework rate** — the percentage of engineering effort spent fixing, redoing, or correcting previous work — is the metric DORA added to their framework in 2025, specifically because AI-assisted development was creating a visibility gap. High rework rates in an agentic workflow typically point to one of two problems: weak specifications (the agent built the wrong thing and it needs to be redone) or inadequate agent context (the agent built something that technically works but doesn't fit the system).  
4. **Test coverage** is a supporting metric, not a primary one. Coverage alone doesn't tell you much — you can have high coverage with weak assertions. But coverage *trends* are informative: if coverage is increasing as agent-generated code increases, the Validate stage is working. If coverage is flat or declining, agents are producing code faster than the test infrastructure can keep up.

#### Agent Autonomy

Autonomy metrics are unique to agentic development. They measure how effectively the team has set up the human-agent division of labor — and they're the metrics most directly tied to maturity curve progression.

1. **Correction loop count** — the number of back-and-forth cycles between a human and an agent before a task is accepted. One shot (agent generates, human accepts) is the ideal. Two passes is normal. Four or five passes means something upstream is broken — the spec, the context, or the task decomposition. Track the average and look for outliers.  
2. **Agent-generated change acceptance rate** — what percentage of agent-generated code changes are accepted into the codebase without significant rework. GitHub's research found that developers retain 88% of Copilot-accepted suggestions in their final submissions. If your team's acceptance rate is significantly lower, it signals a gap in agent coaching or specification quality.  
3. **Organizational alignment** — autonomy metrics that plateau despite good specs and context often trace to organizational misalignment.  To foreshadow that, however, how much role definitions and corresponding titles have updated would certainly be some indicator of maturity.

#### Cost

Cost metrics answer the executive question: "Is this investment paying off?" They need to be honest — which means accounting for the full cost, not just the tool subscription.

1. **Tool cost per engineer** — the total spend on AI coding tools per engineer per month, including subscriptions, token usage, and infrastructure. [Industry benchmarks in 2026](https://keyholesoftware.com/ai-software-development-cost-2026/) put this at $200–600/month on average, with agentic-heavy workflows (Claude Code, high-autonomy agents) running $200–2,000+ depending on usage patterns.  
2. **Cost per accepted feature** — the total cost (tool costs \+ engineer time) to deliver a feature that passes all quality gates and ships to production. This is the metric that connects cost to value. A team that spends less per feature while maintaining quality is getting genuine ROI. A team that spends less per feature while quality degrades is just deferring costs.  
3. **ROI ratio** — the value delivered relative to the investment in agentic tooling and process change. [Industry benchmarks show healthy ROI](https://blog.exceeds.ai/enterprise-ai-coding-roi-studies/) at 2.5-3.5x on average, with top-quartile organizations reaching 4-6x. But be honest about the denominator: [Microsoft's field experiments](https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/mnsc.2025.00535) found an onboarding period before developers see consistent productivity gains, with their [New Future of Work Report](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/new-future-of-work-report-2025/) noting that hidden costs (training, context switching, technical debt from early mistakes) can add 30–40% to first-year spend.

### Reading the Metrics Together

No single dimension tells you whether your agentic adoption is working. The insight comes from reading them in combination:

**Speed up, quality flat or improving** — the ideal outcome. You're delivering faster without sacrificing quality. Your specification and validation practices are keeping pace with your build velocity.

**Speed up, quality down** — the most common failure mode. You're producing more code faster, but defects are increasing, rework is climbing, or escaped bugs are reaching production. This almost always traces back to underinvestment in Define and Validate. The fix isn't better agents; it's better specs and stronger quality gates.

**Autonomy up, correction loops down** — a sign that your agent coaching is working. The context, coding standards, and guardrails you're providing are producing better first-pass output. This is the metric pattern that correlates with maturity curve progression.

**Cost per feature declining, quality stable** — genuine ROI. This is the number that satisfies executives and justifies continued investment.

**Cost per feature declining, quality declining** — false economy. You're spending less per feature but shipping worse software. The cost savings are being consumed downstream by support tickets, production incidents, and customer churn. This is the pattern that erodes trust in the agentic process.

The measurement framework isn't a dashboard to set up and forget. It's a diagnostic practice — something the team reviews regularly, looks for patterns in, and uses to make specific decisions about where to invest next. Are our specs good enough? Is our agent context producing reliable output? Are our quality gates catching the right things? The metrics won't answer those questions directly, but they'll tell you where to look.

## Adapting the Org Structure {#adapting-the-org-structure}

The changes in process, responsibilities, and the nature of the work to be done inevitably net a change in how teams are organized. You can't adopt a fundamentally different development model and keep the same org chart. Or rather, you can — but you'll be fighting the structure at every turn, and the structure will win.

This chapter maps the emerging roles to the Agentic SDLC. These aren't theoretical — they're the positions we've found ourselves building toward as we've operationalized the practices described in this playbook. The roles, the titles, and the expectations that come with them all matter — because when you change what the work *is*, the organizational language needs to change with it.

### The Development Team

The development team in an agentic organization has three core functions: architecture, coaching, and the agent bench. These map primarily to the Shape and Build stages of the SDLC, with the Agentic Architect reaching upstream into Define and the Agent Coach reaching downstream into early validation.

#### Agentic Architect

The Agentic Architect is the role that has changed the most from its traditional counterpart. A conventional software architect designs systems. An Agentic Architect designs systems *and* decomposes them into work packages that agents can execute effectively.

This is the role that owns the Shape stage. The Agentic Architect takes the defined problem — the business goal, the user need, the constraints — and makes critical decisions: what the system boundaries are, where the complexity lives, which components interact and how, and what tradeoffs are acceptable. That's traditional architecture. What's new is the decomposition discipline: breaking the architectural plan into bite-sized, well-bounded tasks with clear interfaces, explicit constraints, and defined acceptance criteria that agents can pick up and execute without constant human steering.

Good decomposition is the second biggest determinant of agentic development success — right behind the quality and completeness of specifications themselves. Specification completeness is the single biggest change in agentic development, and it's the single biggest lever. But decomposition runs a close second: as discussed in Best Practices, AI tools produce high-quality output for well-bounded tasks and structurally shallow output for large, ambiguous ones. The Agentic Architect is the person who makes problems agent-sized — and that requires deep understanding of both the system being built and the capabilities and limitations of the agents doing the building.

The Agentic Architect also reaches upstream into Define, collaborating with product to ensure that specifications are detailed enough to drive the architectural process. And they work closely with the Agent Coach during Shape, aligning on how the decomposed tasks will be assigned, sequenced, and executed. The Architect decides *what* gets built and *how* it's structured. The Coach decides *which agents* build it and *how they're configured* to do it well.

#### Agent Coach

If the Agentic Architect is the strategist, the Agent Coach is the tactician. This is the role that lives in the Build stage — the individual engineer responsible for working with agents day to day, maximizing their productivity, and ensuring code quality.

The Agent Coach is not a traditional developer who happens to use AI tools. The role requires a different skill set. Coaches need to understand how to configure agents for specific tasks, how to provide the right context (coding standards, domain knowledge, architectural constraints), how to evaluate agent output critically, and how to iterate on agent configurations when results aren't meeting the quality bar. They need strong code review skills — the ability to read and assess code they didn't write, spot architectural drift, and catch the subtle logic errors that agents produce when context is thin.

Coaches are also responsible for maintaining and improving the team's agent context — the coding standards documents, semantic data models, business process definitions, and guardrails described in Best Practices. This is ongoing, craft-like work. As the codebase evolves, as new patterns emerge, as agents improve or change behavior across model updates, the context needs to evolve with it. The Coach is the person who notices that agents have started generating a deprecated pattern and updates the standards to correct it, or who realizes that a new domain concept needs to be added to the data model so agents can reason about it correctly.

The Agent Coach role is where most existing senior and mid-level developers will land in an agentic organization. The transition isn't trivial — it requires the identity shift described in the first chapter — but the underlying skills (deep system understanding, code quality judgment, pattern recognition) transfer directly. What changes is the mode of expression: from producing code to coaching the systems that produce it.

#### The Agent Bench

The Agent Bench is a concept that deserves its own explanation, because it changes how teams think about capacity and capability.

In a traditional development team, capacity is a function of headcount. You have six engineers, each with a set of skills and domain knowledge, and work is distributed based on who knows what and who has bandwidth. The bench is the team roster — people.

In an agentic organization, the bench expands to include a roster of configured agents, each tuned for specific types of work. Think of it as a toolbox, but with tools that have judgment. One agent might be configured with deep context on your payment processing domain — the business rules, the regulatory constraints, the integration patterns. Another might be specialized for frontend component generation, loaded with your design system tokens and component library conventions. A third might be tuned for test generation, with access to your testing frameworks, fixture patterns, and coverage requirements.

The bench isn't a collection of generic AI tools. It's a curated set of *specialized capabilities* — agents paired with skills, context, and guardrails that make them effective for specific classes of work. Building the bench is a deliberate investment. Each agent on it represents accumulated context engineering: the coding standards it follows, the domain knowledge it draws on, the examples it's been given, the guardrails that constrain it.

The Agent Coach is the primary builder and maintainer of the bench. When a new feature request comes in, the Coach doesn't just "use AI" — they evaluate the work, identify which agents on the bench are best suited to the tasks, and assemble a game plan: this agent handles the API layer, that one generates the UI components, a third writes the integration tests. The Coach configures, sequences, and orchestrates — reviewing output at each step and adjusting the approach based on what they see.

Over time, the bench becomes a team asset — a form of institutional knowledge encoded not in documentation that nobody reads but in configured agents that actively produce work. New team members don't just inherit a codebase; they inherit a bench of agents that already know how the team works. That's a meaningful accelerator for onboarding and a form of knowledge preservation that traditional organizations struggle with.

The bench also changes how teams think about scaling. Adding capacity isn't just "hire another developer." It might mean building a new agent configuration for an area of the codebase that doesn't have one yet, or deepening the context of an existing agent so it can handle more complex tasks with less human oversight. The economics are different — agent capacity scales with context investment, not with headcount.

### The Validation Team

The Validation Team is a development function whose purpose is to close the loop between specification and proof. This team owns the integrity of the Validate stage — and critically, it reaches back into Define to ensure that validation is possible in the first place.

#### Agentic Validation Architect

The Agentic Validation Architect is a hybrid role — part architect, part coach — focused specifically on the testability and verifiability of the system. This person works at two points in the SDLC:

**Upstream, in Define:** the Validation Architect ensures that requirements and acceptance criteria are detailed enough to generate automated tests. This means the criteria account for both happy and sad paths, edge cases are identified and documented, boundary conditions are explicit, and the spec includes enough structural detail to drive test generation without human interpretation. If the spec isn't testable, the Validation Architect pushes back before the work moves to Shape — because untestable specs produce unvalidated code, and unvalidated code is a liability.

**Downstream, in Validate:** the Validation Architect runs the agents that generate the automated tests. The aspiration — and in mature teams, the reality — is that 100% of tests flow from detailed specifications to automated test generation without human intervention in the test-writing process. The Validation Architect doesn't write tests; they build and maintain the agent configurations, test generation pipelines, and validation frameworks that produce tests from specs. Their judgment is applied to the *system* of validation, not to individual test cases.

This role requires a rare combination of skills: enough architectural depth to understand what needs to be tested and why, enough specification discipline to ensure that requirements are testable, and enough agent coaching ability to build reliable test generation pipelines. It's a demanding role — and in our experience, one of the hardest to fill and most valuable to have.

### Operational Roles

The Run stage of the SDLC doesn't map to a single new role — it's a shared responsibility that spans existing functions. DevOps and SRE teams continue to own infrastructure, deployment pipelines, and platform reliability, but their tooling increasingly includes agent-assisted monitoring, triage, and remediation. Client-facing teams — customer success, support, product — serve as the feedback loop from production back to Define, surfacing the real-world issues and user needs that drive the next cycle of development.

What changes for these teams is less about titles and more about integration. In a mature agentic organization, the Run stage isn't siloed from the development process — production signals flow directly back into specifications, and the agents that monitor production are part of the same context infrastructure as the agents that build and validate the software. The organizational boundary between "we built it" and "we run it" blurs, which is healthy.

### More Than a Title

The titles in this chapter — Agentic Architect, Agent Coach, Agentic Validation Architect — are intentional, and the intentionality matters. It's tempting to treat titles as cosmetic and say "call the roles whatever you want, just cover the functions." We'd push back on that.

Titles signal what the organization values. If you take an existing Senior Developer and add "AI-assisted" responsibilities to their job description, you're telling them — and everyone around them — that the job is fundamentally the same, just with a new tool. That's a Level 3 philosophy: same roles, better tooling. It doesn't create the behavioral shift that an agentic SDLC requires.

The whole argument of this playbook is that we are changing the nature of the work itself — not just how it gets done, but *what* gets done and *who* is responsible for what. An Agent Coach is not a developer who uses AI. They are a person whose primary job is coaching agents, curating context, and maintaining the bench. An Agentic Architect is not a traditional architect with a Copilot subscription. They are a person whose architectural practice is built around decomposition for agent execution. The titles carry that distinction. They signal, to the person in the role and to the organization around them, that something fundamental has changed.

Behavior defaults to structure. If the structure — titles, reporting lines, performance criteria — still says "developer," the behavior will default to development as it's always been done, with AI layered on top. New titles create the space for new behavior. They give people permission to stop doing the old job and start doing the new one.

What also doesn't work is leaving the functions uncovered — assuming that "everyone uses AI" is a sufficient organizational response to the shift. The practices described in this playbook require dedicated ownership. Specification-driven development doesn't happen by accident. Agent context doesn't maintain itself. Quality gates don't materialize from good intentions. Someone needs to own each of these, and the org structure — including the titles — needs to reflect that.

| The Data Science Team Organizations building AI capabilities *into* their products — not just using AI to build them — need a parallel team structure: Data Scientists working on models and algorithms, Data Engineers ensuring data is sourced and structured from all relevant systems, Context Engineers (a specialization focused on RAG, graph-RAG, semantic normalization, and other LLM-specific data challenges), and Prompt Designers who refine the art of getting models to produce consistent, reliable outputs. These roles serve the "Built On" dimension — embedding AI into the product itself — which is the subject of a companion series, not this playbook. |
