# **5\. Getting Started** {#5.-getting-started}

This chapter is about Monday morning — what to actually do, in what order, and how to build momentum without overwhelming a team that's still shipping product on existing deadlines.

Let’s take a moment to stress the amount of change this represents for an engineering organization.  This is truly a “who moved my cheese” moment.  While there are risks to choosing the wrong tools or the wrong process, the biggest risk  is trying to change everything at once. Teams that attempt a wholesale transformation — new tools, new processes, new roles, new expectations — in a single quarter create so much disruption that they lose confidence in the transition before the benefits have time to materialize. The second most common failure is the opposite: buying an AI coding tool, telling everyone to "use it," and calling that adoption. That's Level 2 — individual productivity with no organizational learning.

The path between those extremes is a deliberate, staged approach. But before you build the plan, you have to understand the starting point — and the dynamics that will shape the journey.

## **Assess and Orient First** {#assess-and-orient-first}

Before you touch tooling, before you draw up timelines, before you designate a champion or schedule a kickoff — stop and take an honest look at where you stand.

**Assess your current maturity.** Use the Agentic Maturity Curve to evaluate where your team sits — across each stage of the SDLC, not just in Build. Most teams overestimate their maturity because they conflate individual AI usage with organizational capability. A team where every developer uses Copilot but there are no shared standards, no specification discipline, and no quality gates for agent-generated code is “shadow” ai league, regardless of how productive individuals feel. Be honest about the starting point. It determines everything that follows.

**Set a maturity target.** Identify the next level you're aiming for — not the level you'd like to reach eventually, but the one that represents a realistic near-term goal. For most teams, that means targeting a solid standardized approach: standardized tooling, shared context, explicit quality gates, and a team-level practice rather than a collection of individual habits. Don't try to jump from individual productivity to agentic fluency. The foundations at each level matter, and the teams that build them deliberately move faster in the long run than the teams that rush past them.

**Understand the bias — and why it doesn't matter as much as you think.** There's a growing narrative that newer engineering teams — the ones born in the agentic age, unburdened by years of traditional practice — have a structural advantage. They don't have to unlearn anything. They don't carry the muscle memory of manual workflows or the skepticism that comes from watching previous waves of "transformative" tooling underdeliver.

There's some truth to that. A team that's never known anything but agent-assisted development doesn't face the same change management friction. They won't have engineers who've spent a decade building identity around craftsmanship in a particular language resisting a model where agents write most of the code.

But here's the thing: strong engineering teams win. The fundamentals that make a team excellent — clear thinking about architecture, discipline around quality, the ability to decompose complex problems, deep understanding of their domain — are exactly the skills that the agentic model amplifies. There are no moats around agentic adoption. There are no barriers to entry that a well-run engineering organization can't clear. The teams with strong foundations, strong judgment, and strong culture can close the gap quickly once they orient toward the new model. What they need isn't a head start. What they need is the right vision and the willingness to change how that excellence gets applied.

If you're reading this playbook, you're probably leading or working on an established team. That's not a disadvantage. It's context. The assessment you just did — the honest look at your maturity level — is the starting point. Everything that follows is designed for teams that have real codebases, real customers, real shipping pressure, and real talent that needs to be redirected rather than recruited from scratch.

## **30 / 60 / 90 Plan** {#30-/-60-/-90-plan}

Don't start the clock until assessment is complete. The assessment and target-setting aren't optional preludes — they're the foundation the entire plan rests on. Teams that jump into the 30/60/90 without knowing their starting maturity and their target maturity end up backtracking around day 45, when they realize they standardized on the wrong things or underestimated how much change their team can absorb at once.

One more framing before we begin. Things are moving fast — extraordinarily fast. The technical pieces of agentic adoption compress more with each passing quarter as the tools improve. Parts of what follows can and will move faster than the timeline suggests. But the biggest change isn't technical. It's people and process. And people don't compress. Build time into the plan for the human factor. Change is hard, even when the destination is clearly better.

[![][image8]](https://medium.com/unexpected-leadership/forming-storming-norming-and-performing-5d06d021a969)

If Tuckman's stages of group dynamics — Forming, Storming, Norming, Performing — feel familiar, that's deliberate. Adopting an agentic-first approach is fundamentally a change management initiative. The team isn't just learning new tools; it's renegotiating how work gets done, who does what, and what "good" looks like. That's a group dynamics problem as much as a technical one, and the plan is structured to respect that reality.

### **Days 1–30: Norming**

The first month isn't about changing how the team builds software. It's about building the shared understanding that makes change possible. The goal is alignment: a common vocabulary, a shared experience with the tools, and enough collective comfort that the harder changes in month two have a foundation to land on.

**Establish baseline measurements.** Before you can show improvement, you need to know where you are starting from. Pick a small set of metrics across the five dimensions described in the Measurement section — cycle time, defect rate, a rough sense of agent task completion rate, tool cost per engineer — and capture the current state. These don't need to be precise on day one. They need to exist, so you have something to compare against at day 60 and day 90\.

**Designate a change champion.** Agentic adoption without organizational sponsorship stalls at Level 2 — individual productivity gains that never become team-level capability. Someone needs to own the transition: setting standards, facilitating knowledge sharing, tracking progress, and holding the team accountable for improving their practices over time. This doesn't need to be a new hire. It needs to be a recognized responsibility with dedicated time. The change champion is the person who keeps the 30/60/90 plan on track when the daily pressure of shipping features pushes it to the back burner.

**Run pair sessions — learn together.** The fastest way to build comfort with agentic workflows is structured pairing — an experienced engineer working alongside an agent on a real task, with a colleague observing or participating. This isn't training in the corporate sense. It's shared discovery. The engineer who's already gotten good results from an agent shares that knowledge in real time, and the one who's skeptical or uncertain gets to see the workflow without the pressure of figuring it out alone. Pair sessions build confidence in the process, surface gaps in understanding, and — critically — create shared stories. "Remember when we tried X and the agent did Y?" Those stories become the team's vocabulary for talking about how this works.

**Use agents for research and planning, not production code.** This is the crucial on-ramp. In month one, agents help the team think — they research problems, analyze options, draft plans, summarize technical debt, map dependencies. They don't write the code that ships. This removes the highest-anxiety use case (agents producing production artifacts) while letting the team build fluency with the interaction model. Engineers learn how to prompt effectively, how to evaluate agent output critically, and how to iterate on agent-generated analysis — all skills that transfer directly to the production use cases coming in month two.

The Norming phase is about reducing fear and building trust — trust in the tools, trust in each other's evolving capabilities, and trust that the organization is committed to making this transition work rather than just announcing it.

### **Days 31–60: Storming**

With alignment in place and the team speaking a common language about agents, the second month is where the real friction begins — and that's by design. Storming is where the team confronts the gap between how they've always worked and how the agentic model asks them to work. This is where disagreements surface, where sacred cows get challenged, and where the hard decisions get made. It's uncomfortable, and it's necessary.

**Codify your standards.** Document the coding standards, domain models, business rules, and architectural constraints that your experienced developers carry in their heads. This is the context that agents need to produce output that fits your system. It doesn't need to be exhaustive — a concise, opinionated document that covers the decisions your team has already made is far more useful than a comprehensive but generic guide. Start with the conventions your team enforces most consistently in code review. Those are the ones that matter most, and they're the ones the team already agrees on.  This will also become the baseline for agent development.

This step is also where friction shows up. The process of codifying standards forces conversations the team has been deferring — "Do we actually agree on error handling patterns? Is our API naming convention consistent or just vibes?" — and those conversations can be contentious. That's the storm. Push through it. The standards document that emerges is one of the highest-leverage assets in the agentic model, because it's what allows agents to produce code that looks like your team wrote it.

**Standardize your agent stack.** Pick your tools, configure them for your team, and commit. The value of agentic development compounds when the team shares a common set of agents, context, and practices. Individual engineers using different tools with different configurations is Level 2\. A team operating from a shared, maintained stack is the entry point to Level 3\. This doesn't mean everyone uses the same tool for everything — it means the team has made deliberate choices about which tools to use for which purposes, and those choices are documented and shared.

**Begin building the agent bench.** Start with one or two agent configurations tuned for your most common types of work — maybe one for your primary API layer and one for frontend components. Load them with your coding standards, relevant domain context, and guardrails. The bench doesn't need to be comprehensive yet. It needs to exist as a shared team asset rather than individual engineers maintaining their own configurations in isolation.

**Let agents tackle bug fixes and simple requests.** This is the first time agents produce code that ships. Start bounded: bug fixes with clear reproduction steps, small feature requests with well-defined scope, refactoring tasks with obvious success criteria. These are the tasks where the cost of an agent stumble is low and the learning value is high. The team sees what agents produce, how it compares to human-written code, where it needs correction, and where it surprises with quality or speed. Every bug fix an agent handles is a data point the team uses to calibrate trust.

The Storming phase is uncomfortable because it surfaces real tensions — between engineers who want to move faster and those who want more guardrails, between the excitement of what agents can do and the reality of what they can't yet do reliably, between the old identity of "I write code" and the emerging identity of "I direct code." The change champion earns their title in this phase. Their job is to hold space for the disagreements, keep the team moving forward, and ensure that the friction produces decisions rather than paralysis.

### **Days 61–90: Performing**

With the foundations in place and the team through the hardest adjustment period, the third month is where the practice starts to feel natural — and where the real returns begin to materialize.

**Strengthen quality gates.** Implement the structural checkpoints described in the Agentic SDLC chapter: spec completeness between Define and Shape, architecture review between Shape and Build, automated test coverage within Build, code review between Build and Validate. The gates you stood up informally during Storming now need to be explicit, repeatable, and — where possible — automated. These are what make the agentic process governable at scale, and they're what build the broader organization's trust that agent-generated code is being held to a standard.

**Deepen the agent bench.** The bench that started with one or two configurations in month two should now begin specializing along the contours of your business — not just your tech stack. The most valuable agents in a mature bench aren't the ones that know your ORM or your component library; they're the ones that have become genuine experts in specific modules of your platform. An agent that deeply understands your inventory recommendation engine — its scoring logic, its data inputs, the edge cases that trip it up, the historical decisions about why it works the way it does. An agent that knows your billing module — the entitlement rules, the proration logic, the regulatory constraints. An agent that lives inside your onboarding flow and understands every branch and every conversion-sensitive interaction. This is where the bench transitions from a productivity tool into institutional knowledge — codifying the kind of domain context that traditionally lived in the heads of your longest-tenured engineers and walked out the door when they left. Maintaining these module-specific agents becomes a first-class responsibility, with clear ownership tied to the teams that own the underlying business capabilities.

**Evaluate organizational alignment.** At the 90-day mark, ask the harder questions. Are the team's roles and responsibilities reflecting the agentic SDLC, or is everyone still operating as "developers who use AI tools"? Is there a clear owner for specification quality? For agent context? For the validation pipeline? The answers determine whether your agentic practice continues to mature or plateaus at Level 3\. This is the moment to start the conversation about redefining roles — not necessarily changing titles on day 90, but acknowledging that the work has changed and the structure should follow.

**Agents tackle complex features.** By month three, the team has enough experience, enough bench depth, and enough trust in the quality gates to let agents take on substantial work — full features with multiple components, cross-cutting concerns, meaningful architectural decisions embedded in the implementation. This is where the spec-driven workflow becomes essential: outcomes, scope boundaries, constraints, prior decisions, task breakdown, and verification criteria. The specification is what makes complex agent-driven work governable. Without it, complexity and agent autonomy produce chaos. With it, they produce leverage.

## **Staffing Strategy: Building Through the Draft** {#staffing-strategy:-building-through-the-draft}

So, what happens to junior engineers?

The roles that an agentic organization needs — the Agentic Architects who decompose systems for agent execution, the Agent Coaches who curate context and maintain the bench, the Validation Architects who design quality gates — all require substantial judgment, system-level understanding, and the ability to evaluate code critically. These are senior competencies. And if agents are doing the production work that junior engineers traditionally used to learn on, where does the next generation come from?

This isn't an abstract concern. Entry-level developer hiring has declined sharply — [down as much as 67% depending on geography and measurement](https://byteiota.com/junior-developer-extinction-67-hiring-collapse-explained/) since 2022, with [actual hiring into entry-level roles dropping roughly 73%](https://hakia.com/news/junior-developer-crisis-2026/) even as job *postings* labeled "entry-level" have increased.— and the traditional on-ramp of "write simple code, get feedback, write harder code" is being compressed out of existence. The industry needs to design a new growth path intentionally, or it will face a judgment drought in five years: plenty of agents that can generate code, and nobody left who knows whether the code is any good.

The answer isn't to stop hiring juniors. It's to build through the draft — to find good talent, bring them into the organization with a deliberate development plan, and grow them into the senior roles the agentic model demands. Think of it as a succession pipeline: you're not just filling today's seats, you're mining for rising stars who will become tomorrow's Architects and Coaches.

We'd propose a three-stage growth model mapped to the agentic SDLC:

**Stage 1: Validation Apprentice.** The natural entry point for junior talent is the Validate stage — learning to assess quality before learning to produce it. A Validation Apprentice works alongside the Agentic Validation Architect, reviewing agent-generated test suites, evaluating whether acceptance criteria are actually being tested, running quality gates, and flagging gaps. This is where you develop the most critical skill in an agentic organization: the ability to look at output you didn't produce and determine whether it's correct, complete, and safe. It also builds deep familiarity with specifications and what makes them testable — knowledge that pays off at every later stage.

**Stage 2: Junior Agent Coach.** Once a Validation Apprentice has internalized what "good" looks like, they move into coaching agents on well-bounded, lower-risk tasks under the supervision of a senior Coach. This is the stage where they learn the codebase — not by writing every line, but by reviewing agent output, iterating on agent context, and developing the pattern recognition that comes from seeing hundreds of agent-generated implementations across the same system. They maintain portions of the agent bench, update coding standards when they spot drift, and build the craft of context engineering through repetition.

**Stage 3: Coach to Architect track.** From Junior Agent Coach, the growth path forks. Engineers who develop strong system-level thinking and decomposition instincts move toward the Agentic Architect track. Engineers who develop deep expertise in agent coaching, bench curation, and context engineering become senior Agent Coaches. Both paths require the same foundation: the judgment that comes from having evaluated, corrected, and improved agent output across enough tasks to develop genuine expertise.

The key insight is that the learning model inverts. Traditionally, you learned by doing — writing code and getting feedback. In the agentic model, you learn by evaluating — assessing output and developing judgment. This isn't a lesser form of learning. Doctors learn through clinical rotations, not by performing solo surgeries on day one. Pilots learn in simulators with instructors before they fly alone. The pattern of learning through supervised evaluation of complex output, rather than through unsupervised production of simple output, is well-established in other high-stakes professions. Software engineering is catching up.

What doesn't work is skipping this problem — hiring only experienced engineers, assuming agents will fill the junior gap, and discovering in a few years that there's nobody in the pipeline who has developed the judgment to be an Architect or a senior Coach. The organizations that invest in structured junior growth paths now will have a meaningful talent advantage later. Build through the draft. It's how winning organizations sustain themselves.

# 

# **Conclusion** {#conclusion}

This playbook started with a simple observation: AI has become the principal author of code. Not a helper, not an autocomplete — the primary producer. That shift has already happened. The teams reading this are the same teams that were building software last year and the year before. The customers are the same. The products are the same. What's changed is how the work gets done, and which parts of the work matter most.

### The Argument in Brief

AI's compression of the Build step — from days to hours, from hours to minutes — is the catalyst, but it's not the story. The story is what that compression reveals. When code production is no longer the bottleneck, every weakness upstream and downstream becomes visible: vague requirements that a human developer would have interpreted charitably but an agent implements literally, architectural assumptions that were never documented because "everyone knows," test coverage that depended on the developer's conscience rather than a structural gate, operational readiness that was someone's side-of-desk responsibility rather than a first-class discipline.

The software development lifecycle hasn't gone away. Define, Shape, Build, Validate, Run — all five stages still exist, and all five still matter. But the center of gravity has shifted. Build has been compressed. The stages that were historically underfunded — specification, architecture, validation, operational readiness — are now the stages that determine whether you ship quality software or just ship a lot of code.

This shift creates a new bottleneck, and it's not a technology problem. It's a judgment problem. The constraint has moved from "can we produce the code?" to three deeply human capabilities: the quality of specifications that tell agents what to build, the effectiveness of the coaching that gives agents the context to build it well, and the rigor of the human gatekeepers who decide whether the output is good enough to ship.

### Change Happens in Stages

None of this happens overnight, and it shouldn't. The maturity curve we described in Chapter 6 exists because agentic adoption is a gradient, not a switch. Teams move from ad hoc AI usage (Level 1\) through individual productivity gains (Level 2), to standardized tooling and shared practices (Level 3), to agent-assisted workflows with real autonomy (Level 4), and eventually — for organizations that choose to go there — to agent-native engineering (Level 5).

Each level requires its own investments: Level 3 needs standardized tools and shared context. Level 4 needs specification discipline, structured quality gates, and new organizational roles. Level 5 needs deep trust in the process and a fully adapted talent pipeline. The teams that stall are the ones that adopt the tools without changing the process. The teams that advance are the ones that recognize the tools are only as good as the workflow they're embedded in.

The measurement framework matters here too. Speed, quality, agent autonomy, cost, organizational adaptation — these five dimensions tell you whether you're actually improving or just getting busier. The vanity metrics are seductive. More code generated, more tokens consumed, more PRs merged — none of these tell you whether the software is better. The teams that measure leverage instead of activity are the ones that build genuine, compounding capability.

### The Human Role: Central, Elevated, Changed

The human role in an agentic organization is not diminished — it's elevated. But elevation requires change, and change is uncomfortable. As we discussed in the opening chapter, the identity shift from "I write code" to "I direct systems that write code" is real, and it touches something deeper than skill sets. It touches how engineers see themselves and their value.

The new roles — Agentic Architect, Agent Coach, Agentic Validation Architect — are not cosmetic rebrands of existing positions. They represent a fundamentally different relationship to the work. The Architect decomposes problems into agent-executable packages. The Coach curates context, maintains the agent bench, and iterates on agent configurations until the output meets the quality bar. The Validation Architect ensures that specifications are testable and that automated validation flows from requirements to proof without human intervention in the test-writing process.

These roles require judgment — the kind that comes from understanding the customer, the domain, the constraints that aren't written down, and the history that informs the present. Agents don't have that. They have speed, thoroughness, and pattern recognition. Humans have context, values, and accountability. The organizations that understand this distinction — that invest in the judgment layer as aggressively as they invest in the execution layer — will build better software with teams that are more fulfilled in their work.

### The Goal

The goal is not to replace software teams with agents. It never was. The goal is to redesign how teams work so that humans and agents each do the work they are best suited to do.

Agents are suited to execution — generating code, expanding test scenarios, monitoring systems, surfacing patterns. They are fast, tireless, thorough, and improving rapidly. Humans are suited to judgment — deciding what matters, weighing tradeoffs, assessing risk, and holding accountability for outcomes that affect real people. The organizations that get this division right will build better software, faster, with teams that spend their energy on the work that actually requires human intelligence.

The playbook is here. The tools exist. The teams are the same ones that have been building great software all along. What's new is the opportunity — and the challenge — of learning to work differently.
